name: Kautz Glacier / Kautz Couloir
watch_out: Seracs of the Kautz Ice Cliff present major icefall hazard, especially on descent around Camp Hazard—large ice chunks regularly fall thousands of feet down couloir; position quickly and stay compact with party
Multiple significant crevasses with thin snow bridges throughout middle glacier section—bridges collapse with daily warming cycles and climber weight; probe continuously and belay crossings in doubt
AI2 ice climbing with rotten, wet suspect ice quality—poor tool and screw placements on thick ice pitches; placement failures have serious consequences; use redundant anchors
Descent via Ingraham route passes under seracs during late afternoon—unnerving exposure to falling ice; time descent for cooler morning hours only
Penitentes (snow spikes) cover upper Nisqually and upper Kautz sections—exhausting trail breaking through knee-deep snow formations; altitude combined with poor footwork creates summit bid failures
Weather exposure with severe wind at Camp Hazard altitude (approximately 10,500 feet)—teams blown off mountain in high wind conditions; retreat decision required before summit push
Complex crevasse route-finding on Ingraham Glacier—ladders move and boot pack reroutes overnight; in whiteout visibility becomes critical survival hazard
Crumbly rock sections on approach—volcanic debris creates unreliable rock anchors and loose material on rappel routes; verify all anchor placements before committing weight
Descent slushy snowfield conditions in afternoon on Muir Snowfield—melting creates collapse risk and difficult descending on weakened snow; start descent before 2 PM
seasonal: Best May-June when ice consolidates; avoid July+ when crevasses become massive and icefall risk peaks with melt cycles; early season (April-May) presents sustained wind exposure at high altitude
technical_profile: 5-6 hour ice/glacier climb with 3-4 pitches of AI2-3 ice climbing; approach via Camp Schurman or Camp Hazard; total vertical gain 3,500-4,000 ft; requires solid crevasse rescue skills and glacier travel proficiency

name: Tahoma Glacier
watch_out: Complex crevasse navigation throughout entire route—most crevasses unconcealed with variable snow bridge conditions; lack of previous tracks requires careful routefinding and continuous probing
Serac fall objective danger from ice cliffs above glacier; time climbing to early morning hours to minimize melt-related icefall; position away from direct fall lines from above
Highly variable crevasse patterns year-to-year—previous tracks and route assumptions may not apply; route-finding challenges in whiteout conditions where visual landmarks are minimal

Terrain trap potential if avalanche occurs on surrounding steep slopes above 9,000-10,000 feet—slopes to sides feed debris into glacier proper; monitor snowpack and avoid climbing after recent heavy precipitation
Late season (July+) bare glacier ice becomes extremely hard and slick—crampons essential; blue ice increases fall consequence and decreases screw security; highest rockfall risk from warming mountain
Camping requirement at approximately 10,440 feet below Saint Andrews Rock—site exposed to wind and weather; dehydration and altitude sickness compounded by difficult navigation demands

Multi-day commitment with limited escape options once on upper glacier—weather deterioration or injury at high altitude creates serious rescue logistics challenges; helicopter rescue difficult due to terrain
Traversing high-angle snow (40-60 degrees) with exposed terrain—slip potential on consolidated snow; firm conditions require careful downclimbing if route-finding error occurs
seasonal: Early season (April-May) best when glacier well-filled with continuous snowpack; avoid late season crevasse exposure; route approaches vary seasonally (Emerald Ridge vs Puyallup Cleaver) based on conditions
technical_profile: 3-4 day glacier expedition; 3,000-4,000 ft vertical; multiple rope-up crevasse crossings required; approach via Emerald Ridge (low season) or Puyallup Cleaver to St. Andrews Rock (mid-late season)

name: Nisqually Glacier Route
watch_out: Penitentes (radiation-formed snow spikes) cover upper Nisqually sections at 12,000+ feet—40-60 degree slope with dense spikes creating exhausting trail-breaking; altitude combined with snow depth leads to summit bid failure
Large bergschrund near summit requires careful crossing—may be significant obstacle mid-season with fall hazard potential; probe and belay crossing if uncertain of snow bridge stability
Rockfall from surrounding terrain on exposure zones—afternoon warming increases activity; start before dawn and move efficiently through exposure areas
Crevasses throughout glacier with variable snow bridge reliability—particularly complex on Wilson Glacier approach where multiple crack systems require careful rope team movement
Descent encounters slushy Muir Snowfield (afternoon conditions)—collapse risk on weakened snow and slip hazard even on steep slopes; time descent to complete before afternoon melt accelerates
Long exposure during approach traverse across Nisqually—repeated snow bridge crossings with climbing fatigue accumulated; careful protection placement essential as day wears on
Weather exposure at altitude with rapid deterioration common—whiteout conditions erase visual landmarks making route-finding hazardous on descent; GPS/compass essential
Mandatory helmet use throughout—rockfall and icefall objective hazards present from first pitch to summit; head impacts have serious consequences at altitude
seasonal: Best May-June when conditions consolidate; July+ presents massive crevasses and increased icefall; early season (April-May) features sustained wind at high altitude requiring early summit pushes
technical_profile: 5-7 hour glacier climb from Paradise (5,400 ft) to summit (14,411 ft); approximately 4,000 vertical gain; standard route with most climber traffic; crevasse rescue proficiency required

name: Fryingpan Glacier / Whitman Crest Route
watch_out: Uneven glacier topography with extensive crevasse field—surface crevasses and hidden features create route-finding hazard; particularly dangerous when covered by thin snow bridges that collapse under team weight

Whitman Notch crossing between Fryingpan and Whitman Glaciers presents navigation challenge—correct pass location essential to avoid wandering into steeper glacier sections; visual landmarks minimal in poor visibility
Multiple crevasse rescue scenarios likely on this less-traveled route—fewer established camps mean minimal aid from subsequent parties; self-rescue capability essential
Little Tahoma Peak summit block rock climbing (Class 3-4)—loose volcanic rock prevalent; rockfall hazard from weather action and climber-induced fall lines; secure all protection placements

Descent route complexity—multiple variations available (East Ridge, Fryingpan descent) creating potential for navigation error and unplanned altitude loss; verify descent plan with party before ascending
Exposure on Fryingpan Glacier eastern edge where terrain drops to Cowlitz region—concentration required to maintain safe line away from break-over points
Long day requirements (8-10 hours) from trailhead to summit combined with elevation (11,138 ft on Little Tahoma)—altitude sickness compounded by navigation demands increases error risk late in day
Remote location with minimal rescue access—emergency situation resolution depends entirely on team self-rescue capability; communication challenges due to Mt. Rainier's prominence blocking signals
seasonal: Best May-July when crevasse patterns stable and blue ice begins forming on upper sections; avoid April (unstable snow bridges) and August+ (massive crevasses and icefall risk)
technical_profile: 7-10 hour glacier climb; basic glacier travel with Class 3 rock scramble; AI2 ice at most; approach via Whitman Crest from Westside Road parking (approximately 8 miles, 2,000 ft elevation); Fryingpan Glacier rating Strenuous-3 Technical-3

name: Watusi Rodeo
watch_out: Massive alpine ice pitches (two fat ice pitches with 60+ degree sustained terrain)—excellent conditions in spring create hard ice requiring secure tool placement; tool penetration failure has major fall consequences

Upper rock band transitions requiring bare-hand mixed climbing (low 5th class on exposed rock)—loose volcanic rock prevalent; handholds break under body weight; fall hazard over significant terrain exposure

Objective avalanche hazard on background slopes surrounding lower face—accumulation zone above route; soft slab potential with wind-loaded terrain in January-February; monitor stability before committing
4,500 feet of crampons-required terrain from base to summit—sustained commitment with limited escape; if weather deteriorates mid-route, retreat becomes dangerous in whiteout conditions
Bivy requirements for most ascents due to winter daylight constraints—forced overnight exposure at altitude requires bivy sack preparation; cold injury risk increases with weather deterioration
Route-finding complexity on upper face where multiple variations exist—sparse protection and cairns on exposed terrain; incorrect line leads to steeper sections and exposure to icefall
Marble Creek Cirque approach avalanche terrain—steep avalanche terrain during winter; approach via established track; soft slab formation possible on north aspects following snowstorms
Descent via east ridge with exposure—downclimbing on exposed slab terrain or rappel complexity; rope management critical with potential for snarls on exposed anchor points
seasonal: Best March-April when spring ice consolidates for sustained climbing; avoid January-February high wind/deep snow; December unreliable conditions; May+ routes become mixed scrambling losing technical character
technical_profile: Car-to-car day route (8-10 hours typical); 1,500 feet technical face on 4,500-foot crampons-required terrain; lower sections moderate angle (40-65 degrees), upper sections steeper alpine ice and rock transitions; winter-only viable; helmet mandatory

name: Chair Peak North Face
watch_out: Freeze-thaw cycle dependent ice quality—early season powder-on-rock conditions vs late season consolidated alpine ice present different hazards; early season requires careful downclimbing if unstable; late season blue ice increases fall consequence
One 80-degree crux section (very short) sometimes uniced—requires rock climbing (5.6) when ice unavailable; protection placement critical on this brief exposed pitch
Snow Lake and Source Lake avalanche approach terrain—entire access gully subject to soft slab hazard from surrounding 30-45 degree slopes; avoid climbing within 48 hours of heavy snowfall

Ski resort avalanche blasting near climbing area (Alpental) during season—explosions may trigger slide activity; coordinate timing with resort operations; avoid climbing during official blasting windows
Weather exposure on north-facing aspect—rapid deterioration common; wind loading on north faces during storms; whiteout visibility on descent creates route-finding hazard
Short seasonal window (December-March)—snow coverage and freeze-thaw cycles determine route conditions; January-February most consistent; December and March unreliable ice formation
Accessibility paradox (close to Seattle, ski resort access) creates crowd hazard—rockfall potential from climbers above; position defensively and wear helmet throughout
Descent gully hazard on south side—loose rock and ice debris from climbing above; down-climb with care or execute clean rappels; multiple rappels required with anchor assessment critical
seasonal: December-March with best conditions March (consolidated alpine ice); January-February variable avalanche hazard; avoid April+ when snow coverage transitions to scramble terrain
technical_profile: 3-pitch alpine ice climb; moderate difficulty (Grade II); 50-65 degree terrain with one 80-degree crux; daylight essential (winter daylight constraint); access via I-90 East to Exit 52 (Alpental parking 3,100 ft)

name: Chair Peak Northeast Buttress
watch_out: Most popular alpine ice route in Washington—crowd hazard creates rockfall danger from parties above; position defensively; helmet essential throughout; assess party traffic before committing

NE Buttress orientation receives morning sun—accelerated melt on early ascents (before 5 AM) minimizes sun exposure; afternoon descents encounter slushy/deteriorating conditions; time climb accordingly
Multiple rappels required on descent—anchor assessment critical as rime ice accumulation reduces friction and integrity; test anchors before committing body weight; redundant protection essential
Aesthetic but exposed line—25-65 degree sustained terrain with significant vertical relief; slip on consolidated ice has major consequence; front-pointing technique proficiency required
Wind-loaded terrain vulnerability—north-facing buttress accumulates wind-loaded snow; slab formation possible following winter storms; pre-climb assessment necessary
Avalanche terrain surrounds buttress—30-45 degree slopes on either side; soft slab potential; avoid climbing within 24-48 hours of heavy snow; monitor NWAC forecasts

Ski resort operations impact—Alpental operations may trigger avalanche blasting affecting approach and descent corridors; coordinate timing with resort; avoid climbing during official blasting windows
Relatively short route with limited escape—if weather deteriorates mid-climb, retreat becomes difficult in whiteout; turnaround time discipline essential; descent scouting before descent critical
seasonal: February-March best (consolidated conditions); January unreliable; December rare ice; April+ unreliable; seasonal window compressed; best months have 10-12 hour daylight
technical_profile: 2-3 pitch alpine ice climb; Snoqualmie Pass area classic; close approach; Grade II overall; 50-70 degree ice; short (1-2 hours climbing typically); daylight constraint critical

name: Mount Shuksan North Face
watch_out: Sustained 60-70 degree alpine ice pitches requiring expert front-pointing technique—significant vertical relief with continuous exposure; slip consequence severe; tool penetration failures have serious impact
Seracs hang above glacier approaches—Hanging Glacier serac tracks have fallen thousands of feet; objective danger requires rapid movement through exposure zones; compact party size essential
Spindrift and avalanche activity on precipitous north-facing slopes—regular spindrift courses down face during winter storms; soft slab formation on surrounding 30-45 degree background slopes
Objective hazards (rockfall, icefall, avalanches, slides)—complex maritime alpine environment; rapid weather changes common; retreat decision must come early before high altitude commitment
Poor snow conditions (soft snow) creates terrifying and possibly dangerous experience—hard consolidated snow essential for route viability; warm weather windows render route unsound
Long multi-pitch commitment with limited rest—exposure throughout prevents mental recovery; fatigue errors accumulate as day progresses; multiple bivouac requirement for most teams
North-facing aspect creates rime ice buildup—direct north exposure concentrates wind and moisture; rime reduces friction and increases slipping risk; mist and fog hazard for visibility
Remote location with extreme weather exposure—rapid temperature shifts and wind-loading common; helicopter rescue difficult from north-facing alpine terrain; self-rescue essential
seasonal: Best March-April when alpine ice consolidates; avoid January-February deep snow and wind; December unreliable; May+ routes become mixed scrambles; seasonal window narrow
technical_profile: Multi-pitch alpine ice climb; 60-70 degree sustained terrain; high commitment route; advanced alpinist objective; typically requires bivouac(s); full winter alpine gear essential

name: Eldorado Peak Northwest Ice Couloir
watch_out: Eight 60-meter pitches of continuous alpine ice and snow climbing—sustained commitment with changing conditions pitch-to-pitch; early season thin ice vs late season snow dictates route character and hazards
Knife edge ridge descent after couloir—exposed traverse on corniced ridge with significant drop-off potential; rappel anchors on exposed ridge present rime ice accumulation hazard
East ridge descent route-finding complexity—multiple descent variations available; wrong line selection leads to steep unclimbed terrain or exposure; verify route plan before ascending
Marble Creek Cirque approach avalanche terrain—approach gully subject to soft slab hazard; avoid climbing within 48 hours of heavy snow; route passes through accumulation zone
Seasonal character variation—late fall offers best technical conditions (thin ice) vs late season mostly snow with ice steps; in-season assessment essential
Rime ice buildup on exposed ridges—direct north aspect produces rime during winter storms; reduced friction and visibility hazard; cold and wind create hostile environment
Weather exposure at altitude (8,200+ feet)—rapid deterioration common; wind-loading on north-facing slopes; whiteout conditions erase visual landmarks on descent
Mixed terrain transitions between ice, snow, and rock—variable protection quality across pitch types; mixed climbing sections (M3-4 possible) require rock gear and secure placements
Long day commitment (10+ hours typical)—daylight constraint during winter; partial daylight descent hazard in whiteout conditions; turnaround time discipline essential
seasonal: Best November (after storms, before deep snow) and March-April (consolidated ice); late fall offers technical thin ice; early season powder-on-rock conditions; May+ becomes mixed scramble
technical_profile: 8 pitches of 60-meter climbing; AI3 overall with WI3 ice sections; sustained alpine objective; 1,000 feet vertical in couloir alone; helmet mandatory for icefall/rockfall exposure

name: Argonaut Peak Northeast Couloir
watch_out: Consistent 40-50 degree couloir terrain—steep sections with minimal rest; sustained commitment on constantly inclined terrain; slip potential high on consolidated snow/ice
Middle section melt-out (late season)—upper couloir preserves ice while middle section becomes bare rock/ice transition; conditions highly variable year-to-year; pre-climb reconnaissance essential
Rockfall from upper rock band above couloir—weathering and freeze-thaw action dislodge material; position away from direct fall line; compact party and move efficiently
Wind-loaded background slopes (40-50 degree slabs surrounding couloir)—soft slab avalanche potential; avoid climbing within 24-48 hours of heavy snow; assess snowpack stability
Descent rappel complexity—multiple single-rope rappels required (2-3) on exit couloir section; anchor placement critical on variable rock quality; route-finding essential to locate rappel stations
Upper rock band negotiation—Class 3-4 rock climbing necessary for summit connection; loose rock prevalent; footwork and handhold security essential with significant exposure

Late spring/early season timing best but timing highly variable—May-June offer optimal conditions but year-to-year snowpack variation creates uncertainty; midsummer approach more reliable but loses technical ice
Remote location within Alpine Lakes Wilderness—long approach (8+ miles) with elevation gain (4,000+ feet); rescue access extremely limited; self-rescue essential
seasonal: Best late May-early June when snow consolidates; late fall (September-October) offers technical conditions if snow coverage adequate; mid-summer reliable but approach-dependent
technical_profile: Couloir climb 40-50 degrees; approximately 2,000-2,500 feet of vertical gain in couloir; Class 3-4 rock for summit; full day commitment (8-10 hours typical); requires competent ice axe and crampons technique

name: Mount Olympus Blue Glacier
watch_out: Many crevasses throughout upper glacier halves with extensive crevasse field—dense crack systems with thin snow bridges; continuous probing required; bridges collapse with daily warming cycles and climber weight
Icefalls and bergschrunds on upper glacier—10-foot-wide crevasses to negotiate; serac hazard from ice cliffs above glacier; position parties quickly and move through exposure zones efficiently
Blue Glacier hardening (late season)—bare ice sections become extremely hard mid-summer (July+); crampons essential; blue ice reduces screw placement security and fall consequence becomes major
Fourth of July route (direct from lower glacier) avalanche hazard—steep accumulation zone; soft slab formation possible following storms; Crystal Pass route generally safer but longer
Summit block Class 4 loose rock scramble—final pitch climbs on unstable granite with loose rock prevalent; significant exposure; careful handhold testing essential; helmet mandatory
Crystal Pass approach alternative presents route-finding complexity—longer route alternative; navigation hazard in whiteout conditions; multiple descent options create potential confusion
Remote location with 17+ mile approach via Hoh River—long approach creates time pressure at altitude; rescue logistics extremely complex; self-rescue essential
Rapid weather deterioration common in Olympics—maritime air masses produce sudden storms; whiteout conditions on descent create serious navigation hazard; compass and GPS essential
3-4 day commitment at altitude (10,000+ feet on Blue Glacier)—altitude sickness risk compounded by navigation demands and weather exposure; dehydration significant on long glacier traverses
seasonal: Best July-August when glacier stabilized and weather more stable; avoid June (high avalanche hazard and bergschrund issues); September+ weather deterioration accelerates
technical_profile: Multi-day glacier expedition (3-4 days typical); 17-mile approach from Hoh Ranger Station via Hoh River Trail; AI2-3 overall; 4,000+ vertical gain to glacier; Blue Glacier approach with crevasse rescue proficiency required

name: Forbidden Peak West Ridge
watch_out: 40-50 degree snow and ice in West Ridge Couloir—sustained steep terrain with variable conditions; spring ice consolidation vs winter powder affects difficulty and hazard profile; slip consequence major

Upper rock band (mid-5th class exposed crest to summit)—significant exposure on broken sedimentary rock; loose rock prevalent; handholds and footholds require careful testing; fall hazard with serious consequence
Small glacier below South Face requires crevasse travel—relatively straightforward but requires rope team proficiency; snow bridge stability variable; continuous monitoring essential
Colorado-to-Constance traverse descent complexity—alternate descent via Bailey Range creates potential for navigation error and route-finding hazard in whiteout conditions
Northwest Face approach avalanche exposure—soft slab formation potential on background slopes (30-45 degrees); avoid climbing within 24-48 hours of heavy snow; route passes through accumulation zone
Wind-loading on north-facing couloir—exposed ridge orientation accumulates wind-loaded snow; slab formation possible; traverse terrain exposed to wind-scoured ice and rime
Weather exposure at altitude—rapid deterioration common in North Cascades; whiteout visibility eliminates landmarks; descent route-finding becomes critical hazard in low visibility
Long day commitment with light snow and ice climbing (4-6+ hours typical)—winter daylight constraint forces tactical decisions; partial daylight descent hazard increases error risk
seasonal: Best March-April when ice consolidates but before excessive rockfall from warming; avoid January-February deep snow and wind; May+ too much exposed rock; seasonal window moderate
technical_profile: Grade III overall; approximately 6-8 pitch climbing; 40-50 degree ice in couloir, mid-5th class rock to summit; descent via Colorado Lakes Pass or Bailey Range; Boston Basin approach 8-10 miles; helmet essential for rockfall/icefall
